title: Algorithms and complexity
summary: Big-O notation and counting steps in code, binary search, sorting, hashing and heaps, then recursion, memoisation, dynamic programming and graph search, the algorithm-design toolkit behind the Problem Solving domain.
syllabus: Binary search, sorting, hashing, heaps for top-k

lessons.title: Big-O: how cost grows
lessons.summary: Counting steps as input grows, the common complexity classes, and reading complexity off code.
objectives: You can rank O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2ⁿ)
You can derive the complexity of loops and nested loops
You can distinguish time and space complexity

concepts.name: The growth race
concepts.explain: Big-O describes how the number of steps grows with input size n, ignoring constants and smaller terms. Doubling n doubles O(n) work, quadruples O(n²) work and adds only one step to O(log n). For large n, the class matters far more than the constant factor.
concepts.analogy: Finding a friend at an NDP crowd by checking everyone (O(n)) versus everyone shaking hands with everyone (O(n²)).

visual.shows: Bars or curves of step counts for each complexity class at the chosen n, with a toggle for a log-scale axis and a 'time at 1 microsecond per step' readout.
visual.interaction: Slide n from 10 to 1,000,000; toggle the log scale; hide or show classes.
visual.aha: Exponential and quadratic costs explode while logarithmic ones barely move.

concepts.name: Reading complexity from code
concepts.explain: A loop over n items is O(n); a loop inside a loop over n items is O(n²); a loop that halves its range each time is O(log n); sequential blocks add, nested blocks multiply. Python operations hide costs too: x in list is O(n) but x in set is O(1) on average.
concepts.analogy: Counting how many times the canteen auntie must walk to the kitchen for a given order list.

visual.shows: Code snippets with a live step counter as n varies, and a fitted complexity label (O(n), O(n²), O(log n)).
visual.interaction: Choose a snippet (single loop, nested loop, halving loop, list membership in a loop); slide n; see the count and growth ratio when n doubles.
visual.aha: The doubling test (how much does work grow when n doubles?) reveals complexity instantly.

lessons.title: Searching, sorting, hashing and heaps
lessons.summary: Binary search halves the problem, sorting algorithms trade simplicity for speed, hash tables give constant-time lookup and heaps give the top k cheaply.
objectives: You can explain why binary search is O(log n) and needs sorted data
You can compare O(n²) and O(n log n) sorting
You can explain why dict/set lookups are O(1) on average and when a heap beats sorting

concepts.name: Binary search halves the problem
concepts.explain: In a sorted list, compare the target with the middle item and discard the half that cannot contain it; repeat. A million items need at most about 20 comparisons, because 2²⁰ ≈ 1,000,000.
concepts.analogy: Guessing a number from 1 to 100 with 'higher or lower' hints: start at 50.

visual.shows: A sorted array with low, mid and high pointers; each step greys out the discarded half and logs the comparison.
visual.interaction: Pick a target; step through; compare with a linear-search counter; shuffle the array to see binary search fail.
visual.aha: Halving makes search logarithmic, but only on sorted data.

concepts.name: Sorting algorithms race
concepts.explain: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps neighbours and takes O(n²) comparisons; merge sort splits the list in halves, sorts each and merges them in O(n log n). Python's built-in sort (Timsort) is O(n log n) and should almost always be used.
concepts.analogy: Sorting exam scripts by repeatedly swapping neighbours versus splitting the pile among friends and merging the sorted piles.

visual.shows: Bars being sorted by the chosen algorithm with highlighted comparisons and swaps, and a comparison counter.
visual.interaction: Choose bubble, insertion or merge sort; change n and the initial order (random, nearly sorted, reversed); play.
visual.aha: Divide-and-conquer turns quadratic sorting into n log n.

concepts.name: Hashing for constant-time lookup
concepts.explain: A hash map computes a number from each key to decide which bucket stores it, so lookups go straight to the right bucket on average in O(1). Collisions (two keys in one bucket) are handled but slow things down if there are too many.
concepts.analogy: Pigeonholes in a school staff room labelled by teacher's surname initial.

visual.shows: Keys being hashed into an array of buckets, with collisions chained; a lookup animation goes directly to one bucket.
visual.interaction: Insert keys; change the number of buckets and watch collisions grow; time a lookup.
visual.aha: Hashing trades memory for speed by jumping straight to the answer.

concepts.name: Heaps for top-k
concepts.explain: A min-heap keeps the smallest item at the top and supports insert and remove-smallest in O(log n). To keep the k largest scores from a stream, keep a min-heap of size k and replace its top whenever a bigger score arrives: O(n log k) instead of sorting everything.
concepts.analogy: A leaderboard that only keeps the top 10, kicking out the lowest whenever someone better arrives.

visual.shows: A stream of numbers arriving, a size-k heap drawn as a tree with sift operations, and the current top-k list.
visual.interaction: Play the stream; change k; compare operation counts with full sorting.
visual.aha: You do not need to sort everything to find the best few, a pattern used in beam search and retrieval.

checkpoint_focus: Binary search steps on sorted data
Top-k with a heap in O(n log k)

lessons.title: Recursion, dynamic programming and graph search
lessons.summary: Solving problems by breaking them into subproblems, remembering answers to avoid repeated work, and exploring graphs breadth-first or depth-first.
objectives: You can trace a recursive function
You can explain how memoisation turns exponential recursion into linear time
You can fill a small dynamic-programming table
You can contrast BFS and DFS

concepts.name: Recursion and memoisation
concepts.explain: A recursive function calls itself on smaller inputs until a base case. Naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values exponentially many times; storing each answer the first time (memoisation) makes it O(n).
concepts.analogy: Asking the person in front of you in a queue what their position is, and noting it down so nobody has to ask twice.

visual.shows: The recursion tree for fib(n) with repeated subcalls highlighted in the same colour, and a call counter.
visual.interaction: Slide n; toggle memoisation to see the tree collapse into a chain.
visual.aha: Repeated subproblems are the signal to cache results.

concepts.name: Dynamic programming tables
concepts.explain: Dynamic programming solves a problem by filling a table of answers to subproblems in an order where each entry only depends on ones already filled. Edit distance between two words, for example, fills a grid where each cell takes the cheapest of insert, delete or substitute.
concepts.analogy: Planning the cheapest MRT route by building up the cheapest cost to each station from the start.

visual.shows: The edit-distance grid between two short words, filling cell by cell with arrows to the cell it came from, and the final path traced back.
visual.interaction: Edit the two words; step or play the fill; reveal the alignment.
visual.aha: DP is careful bookkeeping that avoids recomputing overlapping subproblems.

concepts.name: BFS versus DFS
concepts.explain: Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level using a queue, so it finds the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph. Depth-first search follows one path as deep as possible using a stack or recursion, then backtracks. Both visit every node in O(V + E).
concepts.analogy: Searching a shopping mall floor by floor (BFS) versus following one corridor to its end before trying another (DFS).

visual.shows: A small graph (e.g. an MRT-like network) with the frontier, visited nodes and visit order; BFS layers are coloured by distance.
visual.interaction: Pick start and goal; toggle BFS or DFS; play or step.
visual.aha: The data structure (queue or stack) is the only difference, and it changes which path is found first.

checkpoint_focus: BFS finds shortest path in unweighted graphs
